Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 252 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 252 is located in east-central Alberta within the Red Deer-North Saskatchewan 
Region. This unit has Whitford Lake in the north central portion and Vermilion River crossing the eastern portion of 
the area. The unit is approximately 1987 km 2. The habitat is dominated by agricultural land with some areas of 
aspen parkland and grassland. 
 
The most recent previous aerial ungulate survey conducted in this unit was an age -sex survey in 2009. Results of 
previous surveys are summarized in Tables 1-3. 
 
The objective of the survey conducted in January 2020 was to assess the status of the ungulate population in this 
WMU by determining estimates of population size, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of interest, including carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or species at risk. 
 
Survey Method 
 
From January 28-29, 2020, a strip transect survey was conducted flying north-south lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) 
intervals resulting in 21% coverage (with 400 m wide survey strip) for a total linear survey effort of 1226 km (490 
km2). Snow conditions were good in the unit. There was fog on both days that required some lines to be stopped 
slightly before completion. At each observation point, ungulates were counted by species, and, when possible, 
classified by sex and age. 
 
Sex and age classification was determined for moose by identification of vulva patch and size differential of 
cow/calves. Sex and age classification was determined for deer using antlers and size differential between adults and 
fawns. 
 
Density was calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs 
2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the transect lengths varied. 
Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were also 
calculated. A correction factor of 83% for deer detectability was applied to population and density estimates (Habib 
et al. 2012), with a factor of 95% applied to moose density and population estimates. 
 
Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not calculated because the 
design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. 
 
Results 
There were 339 white-tailed deer observed in 76 groups. Of the 339 white-tailed deer observed, 12 (4%) were 
bucks, 103 (30%) were does, 114 (34%) were fawns and 110 (32%) were not classified. Sex and age classification 
was not reliable for this WMU because timing meant that many bucks had already dropped their antlers . The 
average white-tailed deer density was estimated at 0.82 individuals/km 2. Population was estimated at 1627 (Table 
1). 
There were 210 mule deer observed within 33 groups. Of the 210 mule deer identified 19 (9%) were bucks, 73 
(35%) were does, 67 (32%) were fawns and 51 (24%) were not classified. Sex and age classification was not 
reliable for this WMU because timing meant that many bucks had already dropped their antlers . The average mule 
deer density was estimated at 0.48 individuals/km 2. Population was estimated at 958 (Table 2). 
 
There were 95 moose observed within 37 groups. Of the 95 moose identified, 27 (28%) were bulls, 31 (33%) were 
cows, 35 (37%) were calves and 2 (2%) were not classified. The bull:cow ratio was 0.87 and the calf:cow ratio was

1.13 (Table 3). The average moose density was estimated at 0.17 individuals/km 2. Population was estimated at 
336 (Table 3); 98 bulls, 112 cows and 127 calves. 
 
Lastly, there were 24 elk (both on and off transect) observed within 7 groups. Of the 24 elk identified, 2 (8%) were 
bulls, 16 (67%) were cows, 6 (25%) were calves and 0 (0%) were not classified.  
 
We also observed 72 coyotes, 2 red fox, and 50 snow buntings. These are incidental observations only and should 
not be considered minimum total counts.
